newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: Amnesty granted to four South Africa right-wing bombers. [CORRECTED 12:30 GMT]
newsitem.headline: Amnesty granted to four South Africa right-wing bombers. [CORRECTED 12:30 GMT]

text.p: South African Archbishop Desmond Tutu's "truth commission" on Thursday pardoned seven (Corrects from 11) people including four right-wing bombers jailed for human rights abuses during the fight over apartheid.

The commission, which has the power to grant amnesty to perpetrators and limited compensation to their victims, refused to pardon nine other people who had applied for forgiveness claiming their crimes were politically motivated.

Among those given amnesty were four right-wingers convicted of planting bombs shortly after negotiations on democracy began in 1990 between the white-led government of the day and President Nelson Mandela's then newly unbanned African National Congress.
"They walk as if the offence had never happened," the truth commission's deputy chairman Alex Boraine told a news conference.
This meant the pardoned criminals were not open to civil claims from their victims, he told a news conference.
"Amnesty is the price we have had to pay for...our peaceful transition to democracy," he added.

Two far right-wing Afrikaners, members of a group called the National Socialist Partisans, were refused amnesty because they did not support a known political party. Tutu's commission found their group had comprised four members.

Apartheid's foes and defenders have until midnight on Saturday to apply for indemnity from prosecution for crimes committed with a political motive, but Mandela will hear a last-minute plea on Friday to extend the deadline.
"The number of applications has risen incredibly in the last week and even today. It's moving towards 4,000," Boraine said.

Policeman Brian Mitchell, serving a 30-year sentence for organising a massacre in which 11 blacks died in 1988, was freed on Wednesday in a gesture likely to test the limits of South Africa's post-apartheid reconciliation between black and white.
